extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and novice researchers learning to read sources and write research arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assembling, supporting, and documenting a research argument: how to read secondary sources, record and use evidence, construct claims/reasons/warrants, and acknowledge objections so readers will be persuaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions of fact or quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a source's factual or qualitative claim is wrong (e.g., a source claims X is normal/good/significant/useful/moral/interesting, but it isn't).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can reverse the source's claims to state the opposite; use evidence to demonstrate the factual or evaluative error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part–whole contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a source mistakes how the parts of something are related (e.g., a source claims something is part of something else, or that one part relates to another in a certain way, or that every instance has a given part, when it doesn't).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterexamples or analysis of the composition/structure to demonstrate the misrelationship (example: Smith argues sports are crucial to an educated person, but athletics have no place in college).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental or historical contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a source is mistaken about origins or development (e.g., the source claims that X is changing, originated in Y, or develops in a certain way, but it doesn't/it developed differently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical evidence or longitudinal data to correct misstatements about development, trend, or origin (example: Smith argues world population will rise, but it won't).

rubrics_metrics.name: External cause–effect contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a source mistakes a causal relationship (e.g., the source claims A causes B, but evidence shows it doesn't, or that both are caused by C, or that A is not sufficient to cause B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical evidence and causal reasoning to rebut incorrect cause-effect attributions (example: boot camps do not stop juveniles from becoming criminals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions of perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradict a 'standard' view by analyzing the topic from a new context or point of view (social, political, philosophical, historical, economic, ethical, gender-specific, etc.) to reveal a new truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe analysis using a different theoretical or contextual lens to show additional functions or meanings (example: advertising also serves as a laboratory for new art forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary sources for data — verify primary sources when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When using secondary sources for data or quotations, check the primary source if it's available; relying on an important quotation without seeing it in original context is risky and lazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an important quotation is available in original form and context, look it up; record exact wording and context rather than trusting the secondary report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical data only if you can judge collection and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Only use statistical data if you can assess whether they were collected and analyzed appropriately; otherwise, don't rely on them uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure, take courses or consult experts in statistics/probability; know that thresholds for acceptable statistical evidence vary by field and by stakes involved (e.g., psychologist vs FDA demands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must be sufficient and representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't try to find every piece of data, but obtain data that are sufficient and representative for the claim; what counts varies by discipline and question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask instructors or experts for examples of failed arguments due to insufficient/unrepresentative evidence; field norms (e.g., small deep studies vs large sample surveys) determine standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary claims as support only when well-supported or report their reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: You can cite a secondary source's claim to support your argument, but treat it as factual data only if it is supported and widely accepted; otherwise report the source's reasoning and evidence as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim from a secondary source merely shows another researcher agrees with you, cite it as support but not as standalone evidence; include how that source reached its conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read models of argument for structure, not specific ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: You may model the logic or structure of an argument from a secondary source, but do not use its specific ideas (that would be plagiarism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing logic is allowed and common; readers expect originality primarily in problem, claim, and evidence. Optionally note that a prior study makes a similar argumentative move to gain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary sources to define your problem and locate a gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Present your research problem in relation to existing work: describe the line of research your work will replace, correct, refine, or extend and frame the gap your work fills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use earlier studies in your introduction to situate your problem (you may cite them again in the body), e.g., situate a study of the Alamo legend in relation to studies of Arthurian or Grail legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read secondary sources for arguments to respond to
rubrics_metrics.description: Find competing views and alternatives in secondary sources; acknowledge and respond to them to anticipate and answer predictable reader objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't seek only sources that support your claim; contradictory sources reveal likely reader objections and help you strengthen and refine your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take full and systematic notes
rubrics_metrics.description: When recording what you find, take careful notes: record author, short title, page numbers, keywords; separate notes by topic; and clearly distinguish quotations, paraphrases/summaries, and your own thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use headings, different fonts, or colored ink to mark three kinds of notes. At a minimum, include bibliographic data and keywords for later sorting and retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish when to summarize, paraphrase, and quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose summarizing, paraphrasing, or exact quotations depending on how you plan to use a passage: summaries for general points, paraphrase to represent more clearly, quotations when wording is evidence or authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: Summarize for general context (not good evidence); paraphrase for clearer restatement (replace most of original phrasing); quote exactly when words themselves serve as evidence, come from an authority, are striking, or state a view you will dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record exact quotations for evidence and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a passage will be used as evidence, is from an authority, is strikingly original, or states a view you disagree with, record the exact wording now rather than paraphrasing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photocopy passages longer than a few lines; never abbreviate a quotation thinking you can reconstruct it later — misquoting undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the context right when recording and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Record not only what a source says but how the source uses that information: the line of reasoning, whether a point is central or a qualification, and its rhetorical role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the argument's structure (conclusions plus supporting reasons and page references); avoid quoting out of context or reporting minor qualifications as the author's main view (examples contrasting misleading reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record the scope and confidence of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Record distinctions in scope and certainty (e.g., 'causes' vs 'may be a factor' vs 'correlates with') so that you do not overstate what sources claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note hedging language and differences in claim strength when taking notes to preserve intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note why sources agree or disagree
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources concur or conflict, record the reasons: different evidence, theoretical approaches, or interpretations — knowing why matters as much as the disagreement itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the types of evidence and explanatory frameworks used; this comparison can reveal your research problem: which source better respects the evidence?

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-check notes and quotations against sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Always re-check your notes and copied quotations against the original source after drafting to ensure accuracy and avoid confirmation bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you rely heavily on one source, skim its relevant parts after drafting to ensure you've understood it; resist the temptation to read only in favor of your claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the data-dump — organize around the solution and logic
rubrics_metrics.description: When assembling your materials into a paper, organize not by a pile of data but by the solution to your problem and the logic of support — base organization on your argument, not on the data alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the argument early: sketch the claim, reasons, and needed evidence so you know what further research is necessary and avoid wasted effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your readers — read journals, rehearse, and seek feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: To imagine readers' questions, read journals that publish work like yours, rehearse your argument with teachers, and get feedback from people similar to your intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask readers whether the argument makes sense, what is missing, and what they'd like to know; use their reactions to refine clarity and anticipate objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five core elements of a research argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A research argument should answer five reader-centered questions: (1) What is my claim? (2) What reasons support my claim? (3) What evidence supports those reasons? (4) Do I acknowledge alternatives/objections and how do I respond? (5) What principle (warrant) makes my reasons relevant to my claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame your paper as a cooperative conversation with imagined readers, anticipating their predictable questions and answering them in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base claims on reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is a contestable assertion and must be supported by reasons (often more than one); reasons are the immediate support for a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join reasons to claims with because; in detailed arguments, treat each reason as a separate sentence and support it in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base reasons on evidence (distinguish reasons from evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons are mental moves; evidence is what you find 'out there' and make available for readers; reasons must be grounded in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers can check evidence directly; differentiate clearly between your reasons (interpretation) and the data that support them. Evidence should be observable, documented, and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and respond to anticipated objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate reader questions, alternatives, and objections; acknowledge them and respond with arguments, evidence, or concessions as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address plausible counter-explanations (e.g., selection effects) and cite studies that counter these objections; don't omit important opposing views — acknowledging them strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide warrants when relevance is not obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reader might not see how a reason supports a claim, state a general principle (warrant) that justifies connecting that reason to that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warrants must be plausible and, if doubted, themselves supported: readers must accept (1) the warrant, (2) the reason, (3) that the specific instance fits the warrant, and (4) that the consequence fits the claim. State warrants when readers may question relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build complex arguments from simple ones (tiered support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex research arguments are built from multiple simple arguments: several reasons each with evidence, multiple responses to objections, and warrants that may themselves need support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to treat responses and warrants as subclaims requiring their own reasons, evidence, and possibly further warrants and acknowledgments.
